# Diagnosing the "Floor-Hitting" Brake Pedal Post-Bleed

When a brake pedal that was functioning correctly suddenly sinks to the floor immediately after a bleed procedure, the issue is rarely mechanical wear on the calipers or rotors. Instead, this specific symptom points directly to a loss of hydraulic pressure within the system's primary reservoir. While an auto shop teacher might suggest replacing the master cylinder, jumping straight to replacement without verifying the root cause can be wasteful and unnecessary.

The most probable culprit in your scenario is trapped air entering the master cylinder itself during the bleeding process. The braking system relies on Pascal's Law: pressure applied to a confined fluid is transmitted undiminished throughout the fluid. Air bubbles are the enemy here because they are compressible, whereas brake fluid is not. When you pump the pedal with air inside the line, that air compresses before it reaches the calipers, giving a "spongy" feel or a total loss of pressure if the air pocket is large enough to fill the entire stroke.

However, there is a more insidious failure mode specific to Toyota vehicles from this era, including the 2005 Sequoia you are working on: the internal bypass valve within the master cylinder can fail due to contamination or age. If debris in the system lodged inside the unit, it could have jammed the piston internally even before the bleed started. The fact that the pedal was fine "most of the time" suggests intermittent air entrainment or a valve that was marginally sticking, but the act of bleeding—often involving rapid pumping and pressure changes—likely pushed enough fluid past the check valves to expose the bypass mechanism completely.

### Verifying Air vs. Mechanical Failure

Before condemning the master cylinder, you must rule out simple procedural errors that introduce air back into the system. The most common mistake during a brake bleed is failing to keep the reservoir cap sealed or allowing the pump to run dry. If the level of DOT 3 or DOT 4 fluid drops below the min/max marks while the bleeder valves are open, you have pulled fresh air directly from the atmosphere into the master cylinder inlet port.

To diagnose this, inspect the master cylinder reservoir immediately after bleeding.
1. Check the fluid level. If it is low, fill it to the max line without adding any new fluid if possible, as old fluid might already be contaminated with moisture or debris.
2. Perform a static bench test. With the bleeder valves closed and the pedal released, press down firmly on the brake pedal. It should hold firm at about 80–90% of its travel. If it slowly sinks to the floor while you are holding pressure, there is an internal leak in the master cylinder seals (the primary or secondary seal failure).
3. Check for external leaks. Look around the base of the master cylinder where it mounts to the booster and along the flex hoses leading to the calipers. A wet spot here confirms a physical seal breach rather than air entrapment.

### The Role of the Brake Light Switch

You mentioned that the brake light came on during this process. This is likely unrelated to the hydraulic failure but serves as a critical diagnostic clue regarding your bleeding technique. On many Toyotas, the brake light switch is mounted directly under the pedal arm or integrated into the master cylinder assembly. If you disconnected any lines or moved the booster during the bleed, you may have disturbed this switch.

If the switch is now misadjusted and thinks the pedal is depressed when it isn't, your dashboard will show a constant brake warning light. While this doesn't cause the pedal to hit the floor, it indicates that something was physically manipulated on the actuation side of the system. Ensure the switch plunger is free-moving and not caught in the return spring of the booster.

### Final Assessment and Replacement Strategy

If you have topped off the fluid, ensured no leaks are present externally, and confirmed the pedal still sinks without holding pressure during a static test, then the internal seals of the master cylinder are compromised. The bypass valve mechanism is likely stuck open or leaking past the piston cups. In this case, replacing the unit is the correct path forward.

When installing a new master cylinder on a 2005 Sequoia, do not simply bolt it on and fill with fluid. You must bleed that specific wheel circuit first to ensure no air was trapped in the new unit's reservoir before connecting the rest of the system. Additionally, flush the entire system with fresh brake fluid if there is any doubt about contamination from old fluid or debris that might have caused the initial failure.

The trade-off here is cost versus effort. A master cylinder replacement requires bleeding four lines and potentially re-benching the pedal assembly to ensure proper travel height. However, ignoring the internal bypass valve issue will lead to repeated failures. The pedal going to the floor post-bleed is a definitive sign of hydraulic integrity loss inside the reservoir, not just in the lines.
